surface_forms: une femme qui se moque de toi

appraisal_events.evidence: Elle entre « majestueuse, ample et haute dans une longue robe de satin jaune », mais « Sa vue ne me causait plus aucun trouble » ; les invités s'écoulent « en commentant la grande nouvelle : la séparation qu'on disait déjà accomplie entre le duc et la duchesse de Guermantes », et la mère l'a réduite à « une femme qui se moque de toi ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse makes a spectacular entrance whose entire effect the narrator immediately cancels: she has ceased to be an object of desire and is redescribed, through his mother's words, as a woman who merely laughs at him. The surrounding gossip about her separation reinforces the local demotion from idol to subject of salon news.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ne continue pas tes sorties pour rencontrer Mme de Guermantes, tu es la fable de la maison. D'ailleurs, vois comme ta grand'mère est souffrante, tu as vraiment des choses plus sérieuses à faire que de te poster sur le chemin d'une femme qui se moque de toi » ; « comme le médecin qui […] vous guérit d'un mal imaginaire dans lequel vous vous complaisiez, ma mère m'avait réveillé d'un trop long songe ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The mother's rebuke names the narrator the household's laughingstock, invokes his grandmother's illness against him, and diagnoses his passion as a self-indulgent imaginary illness. The narrator ratifies the verdict through the hypnotist and doctor similes, so the passage endorses rather than merely reports the blame.

status_effects.explanation: Her aura collapses within the passage: the majestic apparition provokes no emotion at all, and she is reclassified as a woman who mocks the narrator.
The departing guests make her rumored separation from the duc the great news of the afternoon, turning her into the object of general commentary.
He is declared the joke of his own household and shown to have neglected his sick grandmother for a woman who ridicules him.

The cure is a renunciation: he yields entirely to his mother's diagnosis and spends the following day singing Schubert's « Adieu » in tears, so the loss of the illusion registers locally as mourning rather than gain.
A single speech, likened to a hypnotist's and a physician's intervention, instantly dissolves an obsession the narrator had nursed for months; her authority is total and explicitly endorsed.

ambiguities: The passage's « Mme de Stermaria » does not match any surface form on the reference sheet, which lists only « Mlle de Stermaria » and « M. de Stermaria »; she is very probably the former under a married name, but the identification is left unresolved rather than guessed.

The narrator's disenchantment is genuinely double-valued: the doctor and hypnotist similes present it as a cure (« vous guérit d'un mal imaginaire »), while the closing renunciation and hours of weeping present it as loss. It is read here as a net negative emotional movement because the passage's final movement is mourning, not relief.
